keySentence: You leave Neverland when you grow up but keep its magic.

facts.Page story text 1 (draft, teacher check: Years after her return from Neverland, Wendy had grown up and had a daughter of her own named Jane. Jane listened to her mother's stories about Peter Pan and Tinker Bell with completely shining eyes. She asked the same questions Wendy had once asked and wanted the same adventures for herself too. Wendy realized while telling the stories that not all of Neverland had faded and disappeared from her. The magic had changed shape — it lived now in the stories she told and in her daughter's bright face. It was quieter and smaller than it had been but it was absolutely still there inside her after all. You leave Neverland when you grow up but keep its magic.
facts.Page story text 2 (draft, teacher check: Many years after leaving Neverland, Wendy sat by her daughter's bed and told the old familiar stories again. She had expected them to feel different now — smaller or less real than they had felt when she was young. But something surprising happened as she spoke — the stories felt just as alive as they ever had before. The details she had thought she had forgotten returned with unexpected clarity and warmth as she told them. Tinker Bell's jealousy, Peter's crow, the crocodile's tick — all of it was still there waiting inside her. She realized that Neverland had not left her as completely as she had thought it had during all those years. It had simply moved from the surface of her daily life to somewhere deeper and more permanent inside her. You leave Neverland when you grow up but keep its magic.
facts.Page story text 3 (draft, teacher check: Wendy's discovery that Neverland persists inside her offers the story's most consoling and carefully earned insight. The loss of direct access to childhood's magic is real and the sadness of that loss is legitimate and worth honoring. But Barrie suggests that what seems like loss is partly transformation — the magic does not disappear but relocates. It moves from the realm of direct experience into the realm of memory, imagination, and the stories we tell others. This relocation actually gives the magic a kind of permanence that direct experience, by nature, can never possess. Experiences end but stories endure, and in enduring they become available to people who were not there for the original. Wendy's daughter Jane receives Neverland as a story and finds it just as transforming as the real thing had been. The magic has changed containers but it has not diminished — it has simply found a more durable and portable form. You leave Neverland when you grow up but keep its magic.
